sections.title: The decision
sections.cue: Cue: PM faces the board, then turns to the committee.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: The bank wants an AI platform so employees can build things like customer chatbots, credit tools and fraud tools. Our answer is yes, with conditions. Even a secure platform can host an unfair or unlawful application, so we need to decide what each use is allowed to do. Hung, can you walk us through it?

sections.title: The technical proposal
sections.cue: Cue: Khue hands over to Hung, who presents the proposal confidently.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: Sure. Instead of every team picking its own tool, we build one shared platform with a few approved models, and one gateway that controls access and logs everything. I’d also like the best external models. And credit is the big win: the AI could read documents and draft letters for advisers.

sections.title: Hosting and control
sections.cue: Cue: Security challenges the proposal. Compliance separates platform approval from application approval. The CS pushes back; the PM listens, then decides.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Matthias, you look worried.

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: A bit, yes. With external models, we depend on an outside supplier, and customer data could leave the bank.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: Then we host the models ourselves.

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: That helps, but it’s not enough. Someone could hide instructions in a document the AI reads. If it sees too much, one bad file could leak another team’s data.

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: And it’s not just security. Legally, a chatbot answering questions and a tool judging who gets a loan are very different, even on the same model.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: So approving the platform doesn’t mean approving everything on it.

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: Exactly. Each application gets registered, and we look at it again if its purpose changes.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: Fair enough. But if our own models are too weak, people will just go back to public chatbots.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Good point. So internal hosting is the default, not a rule. External models are fine if they clearly do better, with a contract and no personal data. And search only shows documents you can already open.

sections.title: Credit and meaningful explanations
sections.cue: Cue: The CS explains the opportunity; Ethics challenges the explanation; Compliance gives the legal issue. The PM makes a decision that limits the CS’s proposal and checks that the CS accepts it.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Now, credit. Could we launch document reading and letter drafting straight away?

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: Honestly? Not for the decision itself. Scoring stays with our validated models; the AI would just read documents and rephrase the reasons.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: That’s what worries me.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: Me too, actually. If it misreads a payslip, the assessment changes. And a convincing letter could give reasons the model never used.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: Right. A fluent letter isn’t an explanation. If I’m refused a loan, I need to know what counted against me, and how to fix or challenge it.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: So what would be enough?

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: Plain language, access to the evidence, and a real person who can actually change the decision.

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: And that’s not just ethics, it’s the law. GDPR already applies, and from 20 November 2026, new consumer-credit rules give borrowers a right to an explanation and a review when the assessment involves automated processing. Just signing off the score isn’t a real review.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Then the AI stays out of live credit at launch. We test it offline first, and it only goes live once outputs are validated, explanations match the real assessment, and reviews actually work.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: So the credit benefit comes later.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: It does. Can you live with that?

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: It hurts my business case, but yes. I’d rather launch late than defend a letter I can’t back up.

sections.title: Fraud and the burden of mistakes
sections.cue: Cue: Compliance states the narrow exception. Ethics changes the discussion from classification to customer harm. Keep the disagreement visible.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: What about fraud? Same answer?

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: Not quite. Under the AI Act, fraud detection isn’t in the high-risk credit category. But our other legal duties don’t disappear.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: Legal isn’t the same as fair, though. A false alert can leave someone unable to pay. And since fraud is rare, a model can look accurate while many alerts hit honest customers.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: True. Accuracy on its own doesn’t tell us much here.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: So the real question is who pays for the mistakes.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: And technically, payments are decided in a split second, so the AI shouldn’t block them. It just summarises alerts for investigators; the existing fraud system stays separate.

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: And if the AI goes down, payments still go through.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Good. So we track wrongful blocks, check whether some groups are hit harder, where that’s lawful, and set up an urgent line to fix mistakes. That costs money, and it’s in the proposal.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: I can accept that, if serious harm can trigger a suspension. But customers should still have their own representative here.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: Suspension, agreed. On the customer seat we still disagree, so let’s record your dissent and revisit it after the pilot.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: Fine, as long as it’s on record.

sections.title: Governance and workers
sections.cue: Cue: The CS raises the speed concern. The others answer with how the bank would operate the platform.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: I have one more worry: speed. If every tool needs weeks of approval, teams will just go around us.

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: Then the safe route has to be the fast one. Every tool is registered with an owner, but low-risk ones are approved quickly; only sensitive ones get a full review.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: And what if a team declares the wrong purpose?

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: We spot-check how tools are really used. Registration alone can’t guarantee people are honest.

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: And before launch, we have to consult the works council, so staff know how their work will change.

turns.speaker: Ethics
turns.name: Thiago
turns.text: And give them the time and authority to question the AI. Otherwise they carry the responsibility without the control.

sections.title: The board recommendation
sections.cue: Cue: PM addresses the board. Each final intervention adds a distinct condition. End with the platform/application distinction.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: So, here’s our recommendation. Approve the platform, starting with a pilot of internal assistants. Chatbots only use approved information and can always pass you to a human. Fraud tools only help investigators. Credit waits. And on this platform, no AI scoring customers, blocking payments or reading employees’ emotions. We also pay for testing, support and complaint handling.

turns.speaker: CS
turns.name: Hung
turns.text: And we compare the pilot with how things work today. If it isn’t better, we don’t expand it.

turns.speaker: Security
turns.name: Matthias
turns.text: Every application also needs a tested off switch. We can reduce attacks and leaks, not eliminate them.

turns.speaker: Compliance
turns.name: Yacine
turns.text: And to be clear, these are our own controls, on top of the law. If the purpose, the model or the evidence changes, we review the approval.

turns.speaker: PM
turns.name: Khue
turns.text: So yes, we give up some speed and some early credit value. That’s the price of staying in control. Because approving the platform is not approving every application built on it.

notes: The original banking scenario is unchanged. This is the group’s completed proposed recommendation, not a claim that the bank has implemented it.
Record a full timed run. The section times are rehearsal targets; delivery speed and pauses determine the final duration.
Keep the CS and PM roles distinct: the CS argues for the technology, the PM weighs the objections and decides. The PM limiting the CS’s credit proposal, and the CS accepting it, is a key moment.
Keep the disagreement about the customer representative and the decision to postpone credit. They show a concession and an unresolved trade-off.

Play it as a discussion, not a sequence of speeches: look at the person you are answering, and pick up short replies such as “Exactly”, “Fair enough” or “Me too, actually” without a long pause. Each performer should still adjust the wording to sound like themselves, in line with the course rules on generative AI, without changing the decisions.
Use the oral-defense material for detailed law, evidence, explanation formats and review procedures. The video should summarise the argument.
Video deadline: 4 November 2026, end of day. Project presentation: 6 November 2026, as stated in the instructor’s announcement.
rehearsal.source: Completed script refined from your Phase 3 package and the instructor’s presentation guidance

defense.title: Oral defense: understand and defend the bank’s decision
defense.deadline: Video: 4 November 2026, end of day. Presentation and discussion: 6 November 2026.
defense.basis: Prepared around the instructor’s announcement: the video summarises the case and its difficulties; the discussion tests holistic understanding. A justified decision not to deploy is a valid outcome.
method: Answer the question directly, then give a case-specific reason and a concrete mechanism.
The lead speaker gives the decision; the supporting speaker adds a different perspective.
Distinguish a fact from the case, a legal requirement, a proposed policy and a question still to be tested.
If you do not know, identify the missing point and what evidence would resolve it. Do not improvise a legal rule or a performance number.
decisions: Named owners, registration, access controls, supplier checks, testing and incident procedures.
Approved data and tasks; users verify outputs; no consequential autonomous action.
Approved information, AI disclosure, accessible human escalation; no credit decision or unsupported personalised advice.
Summarises evidence for investigators; cannot block payments. Existing fraud decisions remain separately governed.
Offline extraction and wording tests only; reconsider after validation, faithful explanations and a functioning review process.
LLM scoring, payment blocking, employee emotion recognition
A clear project policy. Legal prohibitions and exceptions have their own scope; not every rejection is a universal legal ban.

roles.name: Project Manager
focus: State the conditional recommendation: what the board is, and is not, approving.
Defend a measurable pilot, the cost of safeguards and the postponement of credit benefits.
Explain how the committee weighed the objections, and which disagreement remains open.

roles.name: Computer Scientist
focus: Explain the application architecture and why the LLM is not the scoring engine.
Explain the technical limits: extraction errors, unfaithful explanations and misleading accuracy on rare fraud.
Accept the PM’s limit on your credit proposal: technical preference does not decide the final recommendation.

roles.name: Compliance Officer
focus: Classify the actual purpose and map the bank’s provider/deployer responsibilities.
Separate GDPR, consumer-credit rights, AI Act duties and the group’s stricter policies.
Explain why meaningful review is more than a signature.

roles.name: AI Ethics Officer
focus: Identify who bears errors and whether they can obtain a correction.
Defend explanation formats and contestation grounds, not just fairness metrics.
Explain worker discretion and the unresolved question of customer representation.

roles.name: Cybersecurity Expert
focus: Trace prompts, retrieval, logs, tools and supplier access.
Explain how injection and permission failures are contained, tested and monitored.
Keep payments and lending operations independent from the LLM gateway.

format: A short plain-language decision notice: outcome, relevant data used and the actual main reasons for that outcome.
An optional detail layer: data sources, how information contributed to the assessment, limitations and a worked illustration where appropriate.
A visible review route: a contact, an accessible non-digital option, how to correct data or submit context, and what happens next.
For the initial credit workflow, use a validated explanation process without an LLM. Any future wording assistant must preserve the actual assessment and pass faithfulness tests.
tradeoffs: Plain language is accessible, but can oversimplify. Link it to a more detailed explanation and a human contact.
Feature-importance charts can help specialists, but may be confusing, unstable or mistaken for causal reasons. They do not replace an intelligible account.
A counterfactual shows how changed inputs could affect this model’s result. It is not a promise of a loan, a causal claim or a fair demand that a person change circumstances beyond their control.

Generated text can improve readability while introducing an unsupported reason or changing emphasis. Use traceability, numerical checks and human evaluation; no single automatic checker proves faithfulness.
Fraud explanations need enough information for a real challenge while protecting others’ data and avoiding disclosure of evasion instructions. The limits require a case-specific legal assessment.
grounds: The bank used incorrect, outdated or another person’s information.
Relevant context was omitted or an inference from the data is inappropriate.
The stated reason does not match the information or process actually used.
The applicant disputes the relevance, proportionality or discriminatory effect of a criterion, even if the data are accurate.
The required procedure was not followed: for example, review was unavailable or consisted of a rubber stamp.
process: Receive the request without requiring the customer to understand the model; provide accessible channels.
Give urgent cases a route to immediate human attention, especially when a payment restriction causes hardship.
A reviewer with authority and adequate time checks the data, reasoning and customer’s account; an LLM does not adjudicate the complaint.
Correct data or reassess the decision where warranted, explain the result, and provide the applicable escalation routes.
Record recurring complaints and reversals so that the committee can change or suspend the application. A review right does not guarantee a favourable lending decision.
example: Hypothetical oral example, not an observed bank result: a rejected applicant says the assessment used an outdated income record.
The notice identifies the income information used and explains its relevance. The applicant can supply a correction and request human review.
The reviewer checks the new evidence and the assessment, then gives a reasoned outcome. The group does not promise that correcting one input automatically secures approval.

unknown: I have not established that point. What I can support is …
The missing fact is … I would check … before deciding.
If that fact changes, the consequence for our recommendation would be …
status: The bank proposes a shared LLM platform for employees; possible applications include chatbots, credit assessment and fraud detection.
Internal hosting by default, limited external use, purpose registration and permission-aware retrieval. These are the group’s choices.
No LLM scoring or payment blocking; suspension power; complaint channels; pilot reviews. Do not present these as universal statutory rules.
Actual costs, productivity gains, adoption, error rates, fairness outcomes and the internal-versus-external model quality gap.
Unverified claims that staff already upload client data; the 97%/5% benchmark; relative wording such as “four weeks away”; unspecified court suspensions.
Task baselines, realistic error analysis, usability and review-process tests, security tests, supplier evidence and operational cost estimates.
rehearsal: Each performer explains the group decision and one concession without reading.
Run the script once with the timer. Keep the CS concession on credit and the Ethics dissent; shorten repetition if the run exceeds 6:40.
Each performer answers three assigned questions in 20–30 seconds, then one follow-up.
Practise the explanation example jointly: CS describes the output, Ethics the challenge, Compliance the right and PM the staffing.
Practise an unknown question. Acknowledge the limit, explain the missing evidence and preserve the conditional recommendation.
Check that all speakers give the same answer on live credit, external personal data, payment blocking and suspension authority.
Verify the uploaded video plays, is no longer than seven minutes and is submitted by 4 November, end of day.

questions.question: What exactly are you asking the board to approve?
answer: A shared platform with application-specific approval, not permission for every employee-built use.
Launch a bounded internal pilot, restrict chat and fraud support, and postpone live LLM credit use.
Fund validation, support and complaint handling; reject LLM scoring and payment blocking on this platform.
questions.followup: Which decision changes if the pilot has little benefit?
questions.avoid: A vague approval of “AI in banking”.

questions.question: Why does a secure platform still need application review?
answer: Security controls access and data flow; it cannot settle whether a purpose is lawful or legitimate.
The same model can answer general questions or influence a credit decision.
Require a named owner, a declared purpose, suitable controls and reassessment when that purpose changes.
questions.followup: Can the gateway discover an undeclared purpose?
questions.avoid: Claiming the gateway understands every employee’s intention.

questions.question: Why not ban LLMs, or let every team choose its own tool?
answer: A ban may forgo useful applications and encourage unapproved tools; we have not measured that behaviour in this bank.
Unrestricted selection makes data flows, responsibilities and supplier dependencies harder to govern.
A bounded shared platform lets the bank test usefulness while enforcing common controls.
questions.followup: What evidence would make a ban or a smaller pilot preferable?
questions.avoid: Stating that shadow AI has already been observed in the supplied case.

questions.question: Why postpone LLM use in credit instead of allowing a human to sign off?
answer: Extraction and wording can influence a consequential decision even if the LLM never produces a score.
Human review needs time, information and authority to correct the assessment.
We postpone this use until validation and borrower review processes work; this is our proposed release decision, not a blanket ban on LLMs in finance.
questions.followup: Would a corrected payslip extraction be enough to release the whole workflow?
questions.avoid: Treating a signature as proof of meaningful review.

questions.question: What would the explanation actually look like?
answer: A short plain-language notice identifies the outcome, the relevant data used and the actual main reasons.
A detail layer and a human contact let the person understand the assessment without reading code.
The same notice explains how to correct information or request review. Initially, credit explanations use the validated non-LLM process.
questions.followup: What does your explanation omit, and can the customer obtain that detail?
questions.avoid: Saying only that the system will be transparent.

questions.question: What are the drawbacks of a letter, a chart and a counterfactual?
answer: A letter can oversimplify; a feature chart may be unintelligible or wrongly read as causal.
A counterfactual describes a model response to changed inputs, but may suggest an impossible or unfair change.
Use a layered explanation tailored to the recipient, test understanding and provide a human review route.
questions.followup: Could a customer understand the text and still be unable to contest it?
questions.avoid: Calling any one explanation format sufficient for every person.

questions.question: On what grounds can a user contest a decision?
answer: They can challenge inaccurate information, missing context, an inappropriate inference or a reason that does not match the actual assessment.
They may also question a criterion’s relevance or discriminatory effect, or whether the review procedure was followed.
The appropriate legal route depends on the decision and facts; our process must accept the concern and give a reasoned response.
questions.followup: What if the data are correct but the customer says the criterion is unfair?
questions.avoid: Limiting contestation to correcting a typo.

questions.question: What is the difference between an explanation and contestability?
answer: An explanation helps someone understand the decision. Contestability lets them challenge it and obtain a meaningful response.
That requires an accessible channel, a reviewer with authority, and the possibility of correction or reassessment.
A fluent letter without those institutional arrangements does not give the customer an effective route to challenge.
questions.followup: Who can reverse the outcome, and what happens if the reviewer disagrees with the model?
questions.avoid: Equating a generated explanation with a remedy.

questions.question: Does human review mean every challenged loan must be approved?
answer: No. Review must consider the customer’s account and correct or reconsider the assessment where warranted.
The bank can maintain a refusal if it is justified through a lawful process and explained appropriately.
Our commitment is to meaningful review and the applicable escalation routes, not a guaranteed favourable decision.
questions.followup: How would you tell the customer that the refusal remains?
questions.avoid: Promising approval after a correction or a counterfactual change.

questions.question: How would you check that an LLM explanation is faithful?
answer: Keep the actual assessment, relevant inputs and validated explanation separate from generated wording.
Check that the wording adds no unsupported reasons or altered numbers; test whether readers understand the same decision.
Automatic checks and human evaluation provide evidence, but neither proves every future output faithful. That is why this use starts offline.
questions.followup: Are the model’s reason codes themselves a complete and valid explanation?
questions.avoid: Assuming a reason-code match proves the whole explanation correct.

questions.question: Why spend on safeguards for fraud if it is outside the credit high-risk category?
answer: The exception is specific to one AI Act category; the customer can still suffer a serious wrongful restriction.
Assess false alarms, customer burden and the speed of correction as well as detection performance.
We propose proportionate safeguards because the harm matters, while checking the other laws that apply.
questions.followup: How would you justify the cost of an urgent correction channel?
questions.avoid: Saying fraud detection is entirely unregulated.

questions.question: If the LLM cannot block payments, who does?
answer: Existing fraud controls remain separate from the LLM investigation assistant.
Those controls still need their own validation, oversight and customer safeguards.
A gateway outage must not itself stop payments or silently redirect decisions to an LLM.
questions.followup: How would you test that separation and the fallback process?
questions.avoid: Implying that removing an LLM solves every risk in fraud decisions.

questions.question: Why can high accuracy be misleading for fraud?
answer: When fraud is rare, predicting “not fraud” for almost everyone can look accurate.
Assess precision, recall, false alarms and the consequences of errors at realistic prevalence.
We have no bank performance figures. Evaluate on suitable held-out data and monitor change over time.
questions.followup: What changes if fraud prevalence increases?
questions.avoid: Using a published benchmark’s performance as a result for this bank.

questions.question: Can you prevent prompt injection completely?
answer: We cannot promise that. Treat retrieved content as untrusted and limit what the model can access or do.
Enforce permissions outside the model, separate sensitive data domains and avoid unnecessary write-capable tools.
Test attacks, monitor failures and make suspension and recovery practical.
questions.followup: Does asking a human to confirm a malicious action always protect the bank?
questions.avoid: Claiming a filter or confirmation button eliminates the threat.

questions.question: Are internal hosting and no personal data in external APIs required by law?
answer: They are our proposed architecture and risk limits, not a general legal prohibition on external APIs.
External processing needs the applicable data-protection, supplier, security and transfer assessments.
We start with a narrow exception for approved tasks without personal data and assess confidentiality as well.
questions.followup: Could confidential business information still be risky without personal data?
questions.avoid: Saying “no personal data” means no remaining obligation.

questions.question: How would you measure unequal harms without misusing sensitive data?
answer: First specify the harm and why group-level analysis is needed; then assess a lawful route and safeguards.
Restrict access, purpose and retention, and consider uncertainty in small groups.
A proxy can be misleading and may itself reveal sensitive information. Neither proxies nor an aggregate fairness score automatically solve the problem.
questions.followup: How would you respond to a disparity based on very few cases?
questions.avoid: Treating bias auditing as unrestricted permission to collect sensitive data.

questions.question: What if an employee labels a credit application as a harmless assistant?
answer: Registration is a control, not a guarantee of honesty or understanding.
Constrain access and tools, check samples of actual use, and require review when purpose or data access changes.
Suspend a misclassified use and investigate the failure; do not claim that prompt inspection reliably detects every misuse.
questions.followup: How do you avoid turning monitoring into excessive employee surveillance?
questions.avoid: Promising that the gateway detects all undeclared uses.

questions.question: What happens during a provider outage or a serious data incident?
answer: Use the tested application-specific fallback or suspend the assistant, with a clear user message.
Keep the existing credit and payment decision processes independent from the LLM service.
Follow the incident process, preserve appropriate evidence, assess notifications and validate recovery before restarting.
questions.followup: Which component is a single point of failure in your design?
questions.avoid: Claiming a kill switch alone ensures resilience.

questions.question: What does this cost, and what benefit would justify it?
answer: We have no case-specific budget or measured return, so we would not invent one.
Cost the infrastructure, platform team, validation, training, supplier work and complaint handling.
Measure task usefulness and error burden against a baseline; reduce or stop a use whose benefit does not justify its cost and harm.
questions.followup: What would you measure in the first pilot?
questions.avoid: Treating another bank’s architecture as proof of productivity here.

questions.question: Your committee is internal. Why should affected people trust it?
answer: That is a real limit in our proposal, and the customer-representative question remains unresolved.
Complaint channels, worker consultation and independent challenge create some routes for affected people to be heard.
They do not fully replace representation in design. Review the committee’s composition using pilot experience and record the dissent.
questions.followup: What would persuade the PM to add an external representative?
questions.avoid: Pretending an ombudsman or a complaint form removes the power imbalance.

questions.question: Why involve the works council before launch?
answer: In the relevant workplace context, French law provides information and consultation duties concerning new technologies and work organisation.
The proposal changes how staff work, verify outputs and bear responsibility, so this belongs in planning before rollout.
Confirm the applicable process and include workers’ concerns about workload, deskilling and discretion.
questions.followup: Does consultation mean workers must approve every individual application?
questions.avoid: Presenting consultation as a universal veto or as optional publicity.

questions.question: Which legal requirements matter before the delayed high-risk duties?
answer: GDPR already applies to personal-data processing and qualifying automated decisions.
AI interaction transparency and the consumer-credit rules have their own application dates.
Check the provision and the use rather than treating one later AI Act date as permission to ignore existing duties.
questions.followup: What is the consumer-credit application date, and is every business loan covered?
questions.avoid: Saying all AI Act or banking duties start on one date.

questions.question: What would make you change your recommendation?
answer: An unacceptable incident, persistent error burden or unusable review process can stop an application.
A pilot that brings little benefit or is routinely bypassed can undermine the platform’s business case.
Stronger validation or a better alternative can also justify expansion or redesign; reopening the decision is part of governance.
questions.followup: Who decides to restart a suspended application?
questions.avoid: Defending the original recommendation regardless of new evidence.

questions.question: The jury asks for a legal deadline or technical result you do not know. What do you say?
answer: I have not verified that specific point, so I would not give a number from memory.
I can explain the relevant risk and identify the provision, test or specialist needed to resolve it.
Our release decision would remain conditional on that check if it could change the outcome.
questions.followup: Can you still make a useful recommendation while acknowledging that limit?
questions.avoid: Inventing a result or giving a confident but unsupported rule.
